lesson.title: The Triple Point: One Address Where Three Phases Meet
lesson.summary: The triple point is the one temperature and pressure at which a substance's solid, liquid, and gas phases all coexist in dynamic equilibrium, making it a fixed, reproducible landmark on any phase diagram.
lesson.body:
A phase diagram maps out which phase of a substance, solid, liquid, or gas, is stable at every combination of temperature and pressure. Three curves divide that map: a solid-liquid melting curve, a liquid-gas boiling curve, and a solid-gas sublimation curve. The triple point is the exact spot where all three curves cross, a single temperature and pressure at which solid, liquid, and gas all exist together in equilibrium.

It helps to picture what "existing together" actually means. At the triple point, the system is not frozen into some static blend of ice, water, and steam sitting side by side forever. Instead, molecules are constantly converting between all three phases, melting and freezing, evaporating and condensing, subliming and depositing, with the rates of every forward and reverse process exactly balanced. Nudge the temperature or pressure even slightly away from that point and the balance breaks: one phase wins and the others disappear. That razor's edge balance is what makes the triple point useful. It is a fixed, reproducible landmark that depends only on the identity of the substance, not on how much of it you have or what container it sits in.

For water, the triple point occurs at 0.01°C (273.16 K) and 611.7 Pa. Converting that pressure to a more familiar unit shows just how low it is: 611.7 Pa divided by 101,325 Pa per atmosphere works out to about 0.00604 atm, roughly half a percent of normal atmospheric pressure. That low pressure is exactly why you cannot casually observe water's triple point at your kitchen sink: it only shows up inside a sealed, evacuated container where the pressure can be controlled independently of temperature.

This fixed point is precise enough to serve as a calibration standard. For much of the twentieth century, the Kelvin temperature scale was defined by declaring water's triple point to be exactly 273.16 K, and every other temperature was measured relative to that single, perfectly reproducible reference.

Comparing substances also explains everyday behavior. Carbon dioxide's triple point sits at about -56.6°C and 5.11 atm, a pressure well above normal atmospheric pressure (1 atm). Because atmospheric pressure never reaches that high at Earth's surface, liquid CO2 simply cannot exist in the open air. Solid CO2, dry ice, has nowhere to go but straight to gas, which is exactly the sublimation you see as dry ice "smokes" without ever forming a puddle.
